cues.why: Enters on 'Deep inside one of those laboratories' -- the sentence that puts us in the room -- and never leaves, because the chapter never leaves. Establishes an occupied but near-empty building at night so that every later silence reads as a room and not as dead air. GAIN 0.08 -> 0.2: Joshua could not hear the room tone at all. 0.08 against a voice reference of 1.0 is roughly -22 dB, which is below the floor of a phone speaker in a room.

The listener hears the chirp, then the narrator says a warning tone chirped. Putting it first makes the sound the event and the narration the confirmation, which is how the scene actually happens to Jack.
The same asset, louder, because the manuscript says the second tone was louder than the first. One generated sound covers both, and the escalation is done with gain rather than with a second file.

The alarm does not stop when the sentence does -- the manuscript has the warning repeating and a second alarm sounding later. A low looping bed under the opening carries that, ducks hard beneath speech, and fades out after 'That's impossible', which is where the scene stops shouting and starts being strange. GAIN 0.2 -> 0.15: Joshua's instruction: turn the alarm bed down. EMPHASIS DROPPED TO 0 on 2026-09-19. The +6.0/+8.3 here were raising the one sound Joshua said he could not hear the narrator past, and they were chosen when the mix was placed by RMS -- which reads this asset 3 to 6 dB quieter than the ear does. With loudness measured properly the category target is already where this moment should sit.
Gives the alarm a physical consequence in a body rather than only on a screen. It is the one sound in the chapter that tells the listener how hard Jack was asleep.
Lands on 'Jack grabbed the keyboard'. Establishes that he is working the problem with his hands, which is what makes the later moment when the cursor moves by itself frightening.
One sharp hit on 'Another alarm sounded'. Distinct from the opening eruption: this is the system finding something new, not the system panicking.
Jack entering a command and running a second search. The manuscript has him working the logs by hand here, and it was silent.
The manuscript says the system beeped and a directory opened by itself. A calm, polite notification is more unsettling here than an alarm would be -- the machine is not warning him, it is working.
It has to sound like the lock worked, or the terminal coming back on by itself is not a violation.
Three seconds of black screen and then the machine wakes itself. Placed after the narration so the listener hears the thing happen having just been told it would not.
Jack's 'Sarah?' has to arrive into an open channel, or the listener does not know he is talking to a wall. This is the cue that changes the acoustic space for the next twenty segments.

A faint live-channel hiss under the whole intercom exchange is the only way to make Sarah read as remote without filtering her approved voice clips. One asset covers twenty segments and nothing of hers is regenerated. GAIN 0.06 -> 0.14: Quieter than the bed he could not hear, so it cannot have been audible either -- and an inaudible intercom bed cannot be judged, which is what he approved it to test.
The manuscript makes static the answer to his question. It is the scene's reply, so it plays before the line that names it.
'Jack tapped the button again' -- the same asset, slightly quieter. The repeat is the information: he is not getting an answer.
Closes the frame cue ch01-070 opened. Without it the listener has no signal that Sarah's channel is gone, and the room he is left alone in is the point of the next four segments.

'Jack froze as a file opened', then TOMBS says Boundary control. Reusing the same calm notification ties this to the directory opening earlier: it is the same intruder, doing the same unhurried thing.
The manuscript puts the door mid-sentence and behind him. The listener should know someone is in the room a beat before Jack does.

Someone entering is one of the few things footsteps are for. Soft rubber soles on a hard floor, because Chapter 1 canon puts her in gray sneakers. Re-anchored 2026-09-26 to the revised line, 'walked straight in ... already crossing toward him'.

'Sarah closed the distance between them' -- the second and last time the chapter hears her walk, carrying her to Jack's shoulder, where she stays. Moved 2026-09-26 from 'as she walked over', which Joshua's revised entrance dropped in favour of this line.

'Jack gave Sarah his chair' -- the same slow roll as the second chair, closing the small exchange that started with 'Can I take your chair?': Jack gives up his seat, physically. Re-anchored 2026-09-26: the chair-exchange rewrite imported on 2026-09-23 removed the line this cue was on, and the drama mix had been skipping it since. Re-anchored 2026-11-01 to 'Jack gave Sarah his chair right away.': the 2026-10 attribution revision split or reworded the old anchor sentence, which left this cue unresolved.

'dragged its chair back, wheels squeaking against the floor' -- the manuscript names the sound. Two people arranging themselves around two workstations; the chairs are how the chapter shows them working as a pair. Re-anchored 2026-09-26: the chair-exchange rewrite imported on 2026-09-23 removed the line this cue was on, and the drama mix had been skipping it since. Re-anchored 2026-11-01 to 'He crossed to the next workstation and dragged its chair back': the 2026-10 attribution revision split or reworded the old anchor sentence, which left this cue unresolved.

'Sarah was already typing' -- the moment the competent one takes over. Marking who has a keyboard is the scene's quiet shift of authority. Re-anchored 2026-09-26: the chair-exchange rewrite imported on 2026-09-23 removed the line this cue was on, and the drama mix had been skipping it since.

Sarah opening the connection history on her screen. She has her own console now and the scene should keep saying so. Re-anchored 2026-09-26: the chair-exchange rewrite imported on 2026-09-23 removed the line this cue was on, and the drama mix had been skipping it since.

'Jack pulled up the TOMBS directory again, tracing back through what had changed' -- the longest stretch of work in the scene, now on Jack's keyboard beside hers, and it had no sound under it. Re-anchored 2026-09-26: the chair-exchange rewrite imported on 2026-09-23 removed the line this cue was on, and the drama mix had been skipping it since. Re-anchored 2026-11-01 to 'He pulled up the TOMBS directory again': the 2026-10 attribution revision split or reworded the old anchor sentence, which left this cue unresolved.
The narration says plainly that she kept typing. Quiet, because it is under a line of banter rather than under the investigation.

Sarah going back to work after the exchange about the baby. Anchored to '...then returned to typing', which is where she resumes. It moved here on 2026-09-21 from 'Sarah returned to the keyboard', whose replacement reads 'Sarah's hands went still' -- keyboard clatter on that line would contradict the sentence carrying it, and the stillness is the beat before her reply. Re-anchored 2026-11-01 to 'Then she returned to typing.': the 2026-10 attribution revision split or reworded the old anchor sentence, which left this cue unresolved.

The manuscript says a new warning tone interrupted them, so the tone must arrive before the narration, into the middle of the warmest moment in the chapter. Same asset as the earlier alert -- the same machine is calling again.

The array waking up, ONCE, from the remote initialization request. It used to sustain to the end of the chapter, and that was the same mistake chapters 2 and 3 carried: this asset is a 20-second RISE, a bed loops, so it climbed, snapped back and climbed again under the last thirty segments. A rise played once is what the moment actually is -- something enormous starting -- and the chapter ends before it would have needed to repeat.
The refusal tone before TOMBS says Request denied, so the system rejects him and then explains itself.

The second occurrence of the same clip, and the same asset again. Hearing the identical refusal twice is the information: he tried again and got exactly nowhere. This cue is why anchors carry an occurrence number.
Jack entering his administrator credentials. Slightly louder than the rest: this is the keystroke the chapter turns on, and the refusal answers it.

The chapter's turn. Being locked out is not the same event as being refused, and it should not sound like it -- heavier, lower, final. After this the sound design gets out of the way and leaves the last nine segments to two voices and the rising array.
“Jack tried his credentials again.” The same sound a second time is the information, exactly as the two denial tones are.

_comment: Ambience was switched OFF on 2026-09-18 while Joshua had no bed he liked, and back
ON the same day when he supplied one: amb_computer_lab, a real recorded computer
room. Both the browser and the exported mp3 read this switch, so the page and the
file always agree.
To supply more: story-rules/reference/SUPPLYING_AMBIENCE.md. Every supplied file
must carry a credit block -- validation refuses one without it.
Where each kind of sound sits in the finished mix, in dBFS RMS, with the narration
running about -22. scripts/audio.py retune-cues derives every cue gain from these
and the asset's MEASURED level, so a gain survives its asset being regenerated or
renormalised instead of silently becoming wrong.
Set after Joshua listened to the first normalised build and said the sound was
super loud. He was right and the numbers said so: nine cues sat at or above the
narrator's own level, including amb_tombs_array_power_rise -- a bed running under
whole chapters at -21 to -23 dBFS -- and two deep vibrations at -18.8, louder than
the voice. That is what happens when assets are lifted 20 to 27 dB and the gains
that were rescuing them are left in place.
A cue may carry `emphasisDb` in its cue sheet to sit above its category, and the
cue sheet is where such a decision belongs: it is about that moment in the story.
LOWERED 3.1 dB (30% in amplitude) on 2026-09-18: Joshua, on the retuned build, still
found the sound too loud against the voices. Applied to every category so the layer
moves as one and the relationships between cues stay as they were.
LOWERED A FURTHER 6 dB on 2026-09-18, third pass. Joshua, after the 30% cut: SFX
still too loud. Beds now sit about 29 dB under the narration and one-shot events
about 23. If that turns out to be too far, raise these five numbers -- nothing else
needs to change, because every gain is derived from them.
AMBIENCE LOWERED A FURTHER 55% (-6.9 dB) on 2026-09-18 before being switched off,
so that whenever it comes back it starts where Joshua asked rather than where the
last pass left it.
A TONE IS NOT A NOISE, and this table targets RMS as though it were. A 500 Hz sine
at -50 dBFS is plainly audible where a broadband bed at -50 is not, so the sirens
needed roughly 14 dB more attenuation than the table gives -- not because the table
is wrong for beds, but because RMS is a poor predictor for anything tonal. When a
future asset is a tone, expect its emphasisDb to be large and negative.
SUPERSEDED on 2026-09-19 by categoryTargetLufs. Kept as the fallback for an
asset measured before loudness was recorded; the retune report names any cue
still landing on it as 'rms fallback'. When no asset reads that way, delete it.
The DRAMA exports. They were 192 kbps STEREO built from sources that are almost
entirely mono -- paying twice the bitrate for a second channel carrying the same
signal. 96 kbps mono is the same audio at half the size: 36.3 MB becomes about 18.
THE VOICE-ONLY EXPORTS ARE DELIBERATELY NOT TOUCHED. combine joins the clips with
`-c copy`, which is lossless and fast, and re-encoding 500 seconds of narration to
save nine megabytes would spend quality on the one thing the whole project is for.
The silence between clips must also stay at the clips' own format or the copy-join
breaks, which is a good reason not to make that number configurable at all.
Raise these if a stereo mix ever becomes real; nothing else needs to change.
Where each kind of sound sits in the finished mix, in LUFS -- BS.1770
integrated loudness -- with the narration at about -20. scripts/audio.py
retune-cues derives every cue gain from these and the asset's MEASURED
loudness, so a gain survives its asset being regenerated or renormalised.
THIS TABLE REPLACES categoryTargetDbfs, AND ONLY THE MEASURE CHANGED. The
numbers are carried across unaltered on purpose: an asset whose RMS and
loudness agree does not move at all, and the ones that do move are exactly
the ones the old measure was placing wrongly.
Joshua, 2026-09-19: 'The first alarm sound in the first chapter is louder
than the narrator's voice... can't hear him talking.' The cue sheet had it
17 dB under the narration and the file disagreed: sfx_console_alarm_erupt
reads -11.5 dBFS RMS and -5.6 LUFS, so it arrived 5.9 dB louder than the
mix believed. Across the whole set RMS minus LUFS runs from +5.6 to -13.1,
an 18.7 dB spread -- while for speech the two agree within a decibel, which
is why measuring effects against a speech reference by RMS looked right for
as long as it did.
The old note here told a future asset that is a tone to expect a large
negative emphasisDb. That advice stands for the SIRENS, whose RMS and
loudness agree to within 0.1 dB and which are intrusive for reasons
loudness does not measure -- but it was the wrong explanation for the
alerts and notify tones, and those no longer need an emphasis at all.

timeline.source: each segment's pause then its clip; the same sum the exports are built with

mixed.indexSource: the manifest timeline, which the mix is built from

voice.indexSource: none: an mp3 -c copy join cannot be addressed by the arithmetic, and summing the parts overstates it because the demuxer applies each clip's gapless padding. Measured, chapter one runs 3.2 s longer than the sum says while a part-by-part index drifts 12 s -- so this file is offered for download and listening, never as something the page indexes into.
